title: How should Settings be structured?
question: The roll assigned a single scrolling page of grouped rows. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: One page of grouped rows
options.lineage: Linear and Vercel settings, raised by a factory readout
options.thesis: Every Factory connection lives on one scroll, grouped by job, with a live status strip you cannot miss.
options.viewport: VASA sidebar stays. Main column opens on a GitHub / this machine / Projects readout, then sticky section labels, then row groups. Incomplete stations expand in place. Appearance is last.
options.risk: A long scroll can bury provider keys if the status strip is not sticky.

raised.raise: A small live readout sits at the top of the scroll, like the amber screen on a desk instrument.
When setup is incomplete, GitHub, this machine, and a Project sit as ordered stations before any preference rows.
Configured items collapse to one-line rows. Only the blocked job stays open.

options.label: Setup story, then quiet
options.lineage: First-run stations that collapse into preferences
options.thesis: Settings is a short story until the Factory can run a Job, then it becomes a quiet preference list.
options.viewport: If GitHub, this machine, or a Project is missing, the page is only those three numbered stations. Once they are done, the same route shows compact rows for providers and appearance.
options.risk: Operators who only need to replace a key must wait through a story they already finished, unless the quiet view is the default after setup.

options.label: Readiness first
options.lineage: Factory health as the first viewport
options.thesis: Open Settings and know in one glance whether a Job can run, then act on the thing that is red.
options.viewport: Three large status tiles fill the first viewport: GitHub, this machine, Projects. Clicking a tile reveals its form below. Appearance is a small control in the header.
options.risk: Tile language can feel like a dashboard instead of settings, and three equal tiles fight for the one action that matters.
